summary:
Astrosim is a browser-based 3D training game that teaches students how astronauts survive on the Moon by letting them do the work themselves. The story starts in 2050, when a team of students is chosen for a lunar mission. Players watch their lander touch down, then control an astronaut who suits up piece by piece, places solar panels in sunlight, builds a regolith shield, runs to shelter during a solar storm, grows food from lunar ice, and handles Moon samples safely.

Our five missions cover suit systems, power, radiation protection, food production and lab safety. Oxygen is shared across the whole game: every mistake costs oxygen and sends the player back to retry that step, so learning comes from seeing the consequences. The solar storm mission is inspired by NASA DONKI space weather alerts, and the mission content draws on NASA Artemis and space station research. The game runs in any browser on desktop or phone, with no install.
details:
What it does and how it works
Astrosim is a browser-based 3D training game for young learners. In the story, a team of students is chosen in 2050 to train for the Moon. The player watches the lander touch down, then controls a 3D astronaut using the keyboard or phone touch controls. A glowing beam and arrow guide the player to each task, and the astronaut physically carries out every action: putting on the suit layer by layer, placing solar panels in sunlight, digging regolith to build a radiation shield, running to shelter during a solar storm, melting ice to grow food, and sealing and analyzing Moon samples.

Benefits and intended impact
Students learn why each step matters by seeing the consequences. Oxygen is shared across all five missions, and each mistake costs 10% oxygen and sends the player back to retry that step. For example, placing a solar panel in a permanently shadowed crater produces no power, and analyzing a sample before sealing the glovebox causes contamination. We want to make space-survival ideas easy to understand for school-age students without needing any textbook or install.

Tools and technologies
HTML, CSS, JavaScript and the Three.js 3D library, running in any modern browser on desktop and phone. We used Claude, an AI assistant, to help write code and text. The solar storm mission is inspired by NASA DONKI space weather alerts.

Creativity and factors we considered
We built the game around doing, not reading: the player performs each task with their astronaut. We balanced realism with clarity, so we simplified some science for learners, such as shield depth and storm timing. The retry rule keeps the game fair, and a skip button on the landing cinematic keeps it quick to replay.

Tools and Languages

TypeScript, React, Vite, Vitest and Testing Library (239 automated tests), ESLint and Prettier, hand-written SVG charts, three.js for the 3D Sim, GitHub Actions for checks. No backend, no accounts, no tracking. Progress is saved only in the player's own browser. The main game works offline; the 3D Sim needs an internet connection to load three.js.
